{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''pseudogroup''' is a set of [[homeomorphisms]] between open sets of a space, satisfying [[group (mathematics)|group]]-like and [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]]-like properties. It is a generalisation of the concept of a [[transformation group]], originating however from the geometric approach of [[Sophus Lie]]<ref>{{Cite book|last=Sophus|first=Lie|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/6056947|title=Theorie der Transformationsgruppen|date=1888–1893|publisher=B.G. Teubner|oclc=6056947}}</ref> to investigate symmetries of differential equations, rather than out of [[abstract algebra]] (such as [[quasigroup]], for example). The modern theory of pseudogroups was developed by [[Élie Cartan]] in the early 1900s.<ref>{{cite journal|first = Élie|last = Cartan|title = Sur la structure des groupes infinis de transformations|journal = [[Annales Scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure]]|year = 1904|volume = 21|pages=153–206|doi = 10.24033/asens.538|url=http://archive.numdam.org/article/ASENS_1904_3_21__153_0.pdf|doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|first = Élie|last = Cartan|title = Les groupes de transformations continus, infinis, simples|journal = Annales Scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure|year = 1909|volume = 26|pages=93–161|doi = 10.24033/asens.603|url=http://archive.numdam.org/article/ASENS_1909_3_26__93_0.pdf|doi-access = free}}</ref>

== Definition ==
A pseudogroup imposes several conditions on sets of [[homeomorphism]]s (respectively, [[Diffeomorphism|diffeomorphisms]]) defined on [[open set]]s {{math|''U''}} of a given [[Euclidean space]] or more generally of a fixed [[topological space]] (respectively, [[Differentiable manifold|smooth manifold]]). Since two homeomorphisms {{math|''h'' : ''U'' → ''V''}} and {{math|''g'' : ''V'' → ''W''}} compose to a homeomorphism from {{math|''U''}} to {{math|''W''}}, one asks that the pseudogroup is closed under composition and inversion. However, unlike those for a group, the axioms defining a pseudogroup are not purely algebraic; the further requirements are related to the possibility of restricting and of patching homeomorphisms (similar to the [[gluing axiom]] for sections of a sheaf).

More precisely, a '''pseudogroup''' on a topological space {{math|''S''}} is a collection {{math|Γ}} of homeomorphisms between open subsets of {{math|''S''}} satisfying the following properties:<ref name="KN">{{cite book|last1=Kobayashi|first1= Shoshichi|author-link=Shoshichi Kobayashi |last2= Nomizu|first2=Katsumi|author2-link=Katsumi Nomizu|title=[[Foundations of Differential Geometry]], Volume I|series=  Wiley Classics Library|publisher=John Wiley & Sons Inc.|location= New York|year= 1963|pages=1–2|isbn=0470496487}}</ref><ref name="Thurston">{{cite book |mr=1435975 |last=Thurston |first= William P. |author-link=William Thurston |title=Three-dimensional geometry and topology |editor=Silvio Levy |series=Princeton Mathematical Series |volume=35 |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=1997 |doi=10.1515/9781400865321 |isbn=0-691-08304-5 |url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/9781400865321/html?lang=en }}</ref>
# The domains of the elements {{math|''g''}} in {{math|Γ}} [[cover (topology)|cover]] {{math|''S''}} ("'''cover'''").
# The restriction of an element {{math|''g''}} in {{math|Γ}} to any open set contained in its domain is also in {{math|Γ}} ("'''restriction'''").
# The composition {{math|''g'' ∘ ''h''}} of two elements of {{math|Γ}}, when defined, is in {{math|Γ}} ("'''composition'''").
# The inverse of an element of {{math|''g''}} is in {{math|Γ}} ("'''inverse'''").
# The property of lying in {{math|Γ}} is local, i.e. if {{math|''g'' : ''U'' → ''V''}} is a homeomorphism between open sets of {{math|''S''}} and {{math|''U''}} is covered by open sets {{math|''U''<sub>''i''</sub>}} with {{math|''g''}} restricted to {{math|''U''<sub>''i''</sub>}} lying in {{math|Γ}} for each {{math|''i''}}, then {{math|''g''}} also lies in {{math|Γ}} ("'''local'''").

As a consequence the '''identity''' homeomorphism of any open subset of {{math|''S''}} lies in {{math|Γ}}.

Similarly, a pseudogroup on a smooth manifold {{math|''X''}} is defined as a collection {{math|Γ}} of diffeomorphisms between open subsets of {{math|''X''}} satisfying analogous properties (where we replace homeomorphisms with diffeomorphisms).<ref>{{cite book |first1=Lynn |last1=Loomis |author1-link=Lynn Loomis |first2=Shlomo |last2=Sternberg |author2-link=Shlomo Sternberg |title=Advanced Calculus |edition=Revised |year=2014 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-4583-93-0 |mr=3222280 |chapter=Differentiable manifolds |pages=364–372 }}</ref>

Two points in {{math|''X''}} are said to be in the same '''orbit''' if an element of {{math|Γ}} sends one to the other. Orbits of a pseudogroup clearly form a partition of {{math|''X''}}; a pseudogroup is called '''transitive''' if it has only one orbit.

== Examples ==
A widespread class of examples is given by pseudogroups preserving a given geometric structure. For instance, if {{math|(''X'', ''g'')}} is a [[Riemannian manifold]], one has the pseudogroup of its local [[Isometry|isometries]]; if {{math|(''X'', ''ω'')}} is a [[symplectic manifold]], one has the pseudogroup of its local [[Symplectomorphism|symplectomorphisms]]; etc. These pseudogroups should be thought as the set of the ''local symmetries'' of these structures.

== Pseudogroups of symmetries and geometric structures ==
Manifolds with additional structures can often be defined using the pseudogroups of symmetries of a fixed local model. More precisely, given a pseudogroup {{math|Γ}}, a [[Atlas (topology)|{{math|Γ}}-atlas]] on a topological space {{math|''S''}} consists of a standard atlas on {{math|''S''}} such that the changes of coordinates (i.e. the transition maps) belong to {{math|Γ}}. An equivalent class of Γ-atlases is also called a '''{{math|Γ}}-structure''' on {{math|''S''}}.

In particular, when {{math|Γ}} is the pseudogroup of all locally defined diffeomorphisms of {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, one recovers the standard notion of a smooth atlas and a [[smooth structure]]. More generally, one can define the following objects as {{math|Γ}}-structures on a topological space {{math|''S''}}:
* [[Flat manifold|flat Riemannian structures]], for {{math|Γ}} pseudogroups of isometries of {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} with the canonical Euclidean metric;
* [[Symplectic structure|symplectic structures]], for {{math|Γ}} the pseudogroup of symplectomorphisms of {{math|'''R'''<sup>2''n''</sup>}} with the canonical symplectic form;
* [[Analytic manifold|analytic structures]], for {{math|Γ}} the pseudogroup of [[Analytic function|(real-)analytic diffeomorphisms]] of {{math|'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}};
* [[Riemann surface|Riemann surfaces]], for {{math|Γ}} the pseudogroup of [[Inverse function|invertible]] [[holomorphic function]]s of a [[complex variable]]. 

More generally, any integrable [[G-structure on a manifold|{{math|''G''}}-structure]] and any [[(G,X)-manifold|{{math|(''G'', ''X'')}}-manifold]] are special cases of {{math|Γ}}-structures, for suitable pseudogroups {{math|Γ}}.

== Pseudogroups and Lie theory ==
In general, pseudogroups were studied as a possible theory of [[Lie_group#Infinite-dimensional_Lie_groups|infinite-dimensional]] [[Lie group]]s. The concept of a '''local Lie group''', namely a pseudogroup of functions defined in [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhoods]] of the origin of a Euclidean space {{math|''E''}}, is actually closer to Lie's original concept of Lie group, in the case where the transformations involved depend on a finite number of [[parameter]]s, than the contemporary definition via [[manifold]]s. One of Cartan's achievements was to clarify the points involved, including the point that a local Lie group always gives rise to a ''global'' group, in the current sense (an analogue of [[Lie's third theorem]], on [[Lie algebra]]s determining a group). The [[formal group]] is yet another approach to the specification of Lie groups, infinitesimally. It is known, however, that ''local [[topological group]]s'' do not necessarily have global counterparts.

Examples of infinite-dimensional pseudogroups abound, beginning with the pseudogroup of all [[diffeomorphism]]s of {{math|''E''}}. The interest is mainly in sub-pseudogroups of the diffeomorphisms, and therefore with objects that have a Lie algebra analogue of [[vector field]]s. Methods proposed by Lie and by Cartan for studying these objects have become more practical given the progress of [[computer algebra]].

In the 1950s, Cartan's theory was reformulated by [[Shiing-Shen Chern]], and a general [[deformation theory]] for pseudogroups was developed by [[Kunihiko Kodaira]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kodaira |first=K. |date=1960 |title=On Deformations of Some Complex Pseudo-Group Structures |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/1970083 |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |volume=71 |issue=2 |pages=224–302 |doi=10.2307/1970083 |jstor=1970083 |issn=0003-486X |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[D. C. Spencer]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Guillemin |first1=Victor |last2=Sternberg |first2=Shlomo |date=1966 |title=Deformation theory of pseudogroup structures |journal=[[Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society]] |issue=64 |pages=0 |doi=10.1090/memo/0064 |issn=0065-9266 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In the 1960s [[homological algebra]] was applied to the basic [[partial differential equation|PDE]] questions of over-determination; however, this revealed that the algebra of the theory is potentially very heavy. In the same decade the interest for [[theoretical physics]] of infinite-dimensional Lie theory appeared for the first time, in the shape of [[current algebra]].

Intuitively, a '''Lie pseudogroup''' should be a pseudogroup which "originates" from a system of PDEs. There are many similar but inequivalent notions in the literature;<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kumpera |first1=Antonio|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1515/9781400881734 |title=Lie Equations, Vol. I |last2=Spencer |first2=Donald Clayton |date=1973-01-01 |publisher=Princeton University Press |doi=10.1515/9781400881734 |isbn=978-1-4008-8173-4 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Singer |first1=I. M. |author-link=Isadore Singer |last2=Sternberg |first2=Shlomo |date=1965 |title=The infinite groups of Lie and Cartan Part I, (The transitive groups) |journal=[[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=1–114 |doi=10.1007/bf02787690 |doi-access= |s2cid=123124081 |issn=0021-7670 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Claude. |first=Albert |url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/715985799 |title=Pseudogroupes de Lie transitifs |date=1984–1987 |publisher=Hermann |oclc=715985799 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kuranishi |first=Masatake |date=1959 |title=On the Local Theory of Continuous Infinite Pseudo Groups I |journal=Nagoya Mathematical Journal |volume=15 |pages=225–260 |doi=10.1017/s0027763000006747 |issn=0027-7630 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Olver |first1=Peter J. |last2=Pohjanpelto |first2=Juha |date=2005 |title=Maurer–Cartan forms and the structure of Lie pseudo-groups |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s00029-005-0008-7 |journal=Selecta Mathematica |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=99–126 |doi=10.1007/s00029-005-0008-7 |s2cid=14712181 |issn=1022-1824 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> the "right" one depends on which application one has in mind. However, all these various approaches involve the (finite- or infinite-dimensional) [[Jet bundle|jet bundles]] of {{math|Γ}}, which are asked to be a [[Lie groupoid]]. In particular, a Lie pseudogroup is called of '''finite order {{math|''k''}}''' if it can be "reconstructed" from the space of its {{math|''k''}}-[[Jet (mathematics)|jets]].
